name: Tyrannosaurus rex
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large herbivores like Triceratops and Edmontosaurus.
discoveryHistory: First discovered by Arthur Lakes in Colorado (1874), later named and described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905.
interestingFacts: ["Delivered the highest estimated bite force of any known terrestrial animal, calculated between 35,000 to 57,000 Newtons, capable of pulverizing cortical bone (Bates & Falkingham 2012).","Rigid cranial architecture featured fused nasal bones, expanded frontals, and an immobile postorbital-jugal complex that resisted enormous torsional stress during bone-crushing bites (Cost et al. 2019).","Robust, blunt-tipped 'banana teeth' possessed deep roots (up to 30 cm total length) and wide cross-sections, allowing them to crack bone rather than slice flesh.","Binocular field of vision spanned 55 degrees—exceeding that of modern hawks—due to its laterally expanded temporal skull region and forward-facing orbits (Stevens 2006).","Preserved fossil integument from multiple skeletal regions (Wyrex specimen) documents micro-tuberculate scale impressions across the neck, pelvis, and tail (Bell et al. 2017)."]
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 8,400 to 14,000 kg depending on study.

name: Triceratops horridus
dietDetails: Low-growing vegetation like ferns, cycads, and palms, cropped with its powerful beak.
discoveryHistory: First found near Denver, Colorado, in 1887 by George Lyman Cannon. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh.
interestingFacts: ["The solid, unperforated parietal-squamosal frill lacked the large open fenestrae present in other ceratopsids, providing structural shielding against frontal horn thrusts during intraspecific combat (Farke et al. 2009).","Brow horns could exceed 1 meter in length and were covered in a keratinous sheath with prominent vascular grooves indicating active epidermal growth.","Massive dental batteries contained hundreds of teeth stacked up to five deep in columns, with self-sharpening enamel surfaces that ground fibrous angiosperms and palms.","Histological growth stages show that the epoccipital bones bordering the frill changed from triangular spikes in juveniles into flattened triangular scallops in mature adults (Horner & Goodwin 2006).","Massive, ball-and-socket occipital condyle allowed an exceptionally wide range of rotational movement for the head relative to the cervical vertebrae."]
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000 kg depending on body mass calculations.

name: Velociraptor mongoliensis
dietDetails: Protoceratops and small desert tetrapods.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Peter Kaisen in 1923 at Flaming Cliffs.
interestingFacts: ["Retractable 9 cm sickle claw on second toe.","Quill knobs on ulna proving presence of feathers.","Slender upturned snout.","The tail was reinforced by long, ossified chevron extensions and hypapophyses, turning the caudal series into a stiffened dynamic stabilizer for sharp turning maneuvers while sprinting (Norell & Makovicky 1999).","The famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil (specimen MPC-D 100/25) preserved a Velociraptor locked in mortal combat with a Protoceratops, frozen mid-strike beneath a collapsing sand dune."]
sizeNotes: Adult length ~2.0m, height ~0.5m, estimated weight ~15kg. Note: Holotype AMNH 6515 and complete Djadochta specimens measure 2.07 m total length, standing 0.5 m at the hip, weighing 14–18 kg (representative 15 kg).

name: Parasaurolophus walkeri
dietDetails: High and low vegetation, conifers, leaves, and twigs, processed with grinding dental batteries.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Alberta, Canada, in 1920 by William Parks. Described in 1922.
interestingFacts: ["The hollow, backwards-curving cranial crest contained internal looping nasal passages stretching up to 2.6 meters, functioning as an acoustic resonating chamber (Weishampel 1981).","CT reconstructions and acoustic modeling show that the internal acoustic passages could resonate low-frequency sound waves around 48–75 Hz, ideal for long-distance forest communication (Sullivan & Williamson 1999).","A pronounced notch in the dorsal neural spines of the neck corresponds to the trajectory of the crest when the head was thrown back during vocalization.","Dental batteries comprised up to 1,000 tightly packed teeth that continuously erupted to grind fibrous conifers, leaves, and twigs.","Preserved skin impressions show small, non-overlapping polygonal scales with uniform tubercle patterning across the flanks."]
sizeNotes: Grew to about 9.5 meters long; weight estimated at 2.5 metric tons. Note: Length of 9.5 m and hip height 3.2 m are well established from holotype ROM 768. The weight of 2,500 kg is an underestimate for an 9.5m hadrosaur; modern volumetric estimates place it at 3,000–3,600 kg (midpoint 3,200 kg).

name: Ankylosaurus magniventris
nameMeaning: Fused lizard with a great belly
dietDetails: Low-growing plants, ferns, and shrubs, cropped with its broad beak.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Barnum Brown in 1906. Described in 1908.
interestingFacts: ["The heavy tail club was formed by interlocking distal caudal vertebrae and four osteodermal plates, capable of generating an impact force exceeding 14,000 Newtons (Arbour & Snively 2009).","The skull was covered in fused cranial osteoderms (caputegulae) that obscured cranial sutures and formed protective armored plates over the nostrils and cheeks.","Possessed complex, looping nasal air passages that conditioned incoming air and aided thermoregulatory cooling of blood flowing to the brain (Miyashita et al. 2011).","The broad, barrel-shaped body was heavily armored with transverse rows of keeled osteoderms embedded in a thick dermal matrix across the neck, back, and hips.","Small, leaf-shaped teeth with denticulate margins were adapted for non-selective low browsing, relying on an enormous fermentation gut to break down vegetation."]
sizeNotes: Ranged from 6 to 8 meters long; weighed roughly 5 to 8 metric tons.

name: Carnotaurus sastrei
dietDetails: Medium-sized herbivores and small dinosaurs in open dry landscapes.
media: [{"url":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/Carnotaurus_TD.png","type":"art","credit":"TotalDino (CC BY 4.0)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carnotaurus_TD.png"},{"url":"https://bbsmxcoywionsvmfznah.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/species-media/29-Carnotaurus.jpg","type":"photo","credit":"Lida Xing and Yi Liu (CC BY 2.5)","sourceUrl":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carnotaurus_life_restoration_(mirrored).jpg"}]
discoveryHistory: Found in Chubut Province, Argentina, by Anselmo Sastre in 1984 during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a pair of prominent, thick frontal horns above the eyes—unique among large theropods—which likely served in blunt head-to-head pushing or display contests (Mazzetta et al. 2004).","Forelimbs were extremely vestigial with four digits, an immobile elbow, and completely reduced forearms, yet retained a flexible ball-and-socket shoulder joint.","Massive caudofemoralis muscles attached to specialized, elevated caudal ribs (cervicalized caudal vertebrae), making Carnotaurus one of the fastest sprint runners among large theropods (Persons & Currie 2011).","Exceptionally preserved skin impressions from the holotype specimen show large, conical studs arranged in irregular longitudinal rows surrounded by smaller basement scales (Hendrickx & Bell 2021).","The skull was short, deep, and heavily fused, with kinetic jaw mechanics specialized for rapid slashing snaps against fast, agile prey."]
sizeNotes: Ranged from 7.5 to 9 meters in length; weight is estimated around 1.35 metric tons. Note: Holotype MACN-CH 894 length is 7.6–8.0 m (midpoint 7.8 m), standing hip height 2.5 m. Volumetric mass range spans 1,350–1,750 kg (representative midpoint 1,500 kg).

name: Quetzalcoatlus northropi
nameMeaning: Named after the Aztec feathered serpent god Quetzalcoatl
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, carrion, and terrestrial prey.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Big Bend National Park, Texas, by Douglas A. Lawson in 1971. Described in 1975.
interestingFacts: ["With an estimated wingspan of 10 to 11 meters (33–36 feet), it was one of the largest flying animals in Earth's history, standing as tall as a modern giraffe on the ground (Padian et al. 2021).","Launched into flight via quadrupedal vaulting, using its immense forelimbs and reinforced wing-finger joints to push explosively off the substrate (Habib 2008).","Possessed an elongated, toothless beak and a stiffened, elongate cervical vertebral column, adapted for terrestrial stalking and snatching small vertebrates in inland floodplain habitats.","Bone walls were ultra-thin (often under 2 mm) with extensive internal trabecular reinforcement and pneumatic foramina connected to a complex respiratory air sac system.","Preserved fossil pycnofibers demonstrate that the body was covered in a dense coat of filamentous insulation for thermoregulation."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 10 to 11 meters; weight estimates range from 70 to 250 kg due to light, air-filled bones. Note: Wingspan 10–11 m. In quadrupedal standing pose, shoulder height is ~3.0 m and head/crest height reaches 5.0 m. Total body length (beak to feet) ~4.5 m. Flight mass consensus is 200–250 kg (representative 220 kg).

name: Pteranodon longiceps
dietDetails: Fishes, squids, and small marine organisms caught by diving.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1870 in the Smoky Hill Chalk of Kansas. It was the first pterosaur found outside Europe.
interestingFacts: ["Displayed dramatic sexual dimorphism: adult males possessed large backward-swept cranial crests and 6-meter wingspans, while females had small, rounded crests and 3.8-meter wingspans (Bennett 1992).","The toothless jaws ended in a sharp, tapered beak with a specialized palate structure adapted for scoop-netting pelagic fish from the surface waters of the Western Interior Seaway.","Metacarpal bones of the wing were longer than the humerus, creating an exceptionally high-aspect-ratio wing specialized for efficient dynamic ocean soaring.","Fossils frequently exhibit fused pelvic and scapulocoracoid elements in fully mature individuals, providing structural rigidity against aerodynamic flight loads.","Possessed an elongated, fused synsacrum of up to 10 vertebrae and a short, stiffened tail that minimized drag during long-distance oceanic glides."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 5.6 meters for females, up to 7.2 meters for males. Weight: ~30 to 90 kg. Note: Wingspan 5.6 m (females) to 6.5–7.0 m (large males). Quadrupedal standing height ~1.5 m, body length ~2.0 m. Modern mass calculations (Witton 2013) demonstrate 50 kg is too heavy for an animal with ultra-thin cortical bone; adult male mass is 30–40 kg (representative 35 kg).

name: Mosasaurus hoffmannii
dietDetails: Fish, ammonites, sharks, plesiosaurs, sea turtles, and even smaller mosasaurs.
discoveryHistory: First found in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in 1764. The skull became famous when French revolutionary forces confiscated it in 1794.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed an intramandibular joint in the lower jaw and a specialized pterygoid tooth battery on the roof of the mouth that held struggling marine prey while swallowing.","Distal tail vertebrae were downturned (hypocercal) and supported a crescent-shaped, shark-like two-lobed caudal tail fin that generated powerful burst propulsion (Lindgren et al. 2013).","Massive conical teeth had faceted enamel surfaces with dual cutting carinae, specialized for crushing ammonite shells, sea turtles, and other marine reptiles.","Sclerotic rings in the orbits were small relative to the skull, indicating an animal adapted for hunting in well-lit epipelagic surface waters rather than deep trenches.","Advanced bone histology and isotopic analysis demonstrate endothermic or gigantothermic metabolic rates, allowing active hunting in diverse water temperatures."]
sizeNotes: Large specimens reached up to 15 to 17 meters in length; weight is estimated at 10 to 15 metric tons.

name: Elasmosaurus platyurus
nameMeaning: Thin-plate lizard with a flat tail
dietDetails: Small bony fish, squids, and shelled cephalopods.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Kansas in 1867 by Theophilus Turner. Described by Edward Drinker Cope, who notoriously reconstructed the fossil with the head on the tail end.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed an extraordinary neck containing 72 cervical vertebrae—more than any other known animal—accounting for more than half of its total 10.3-meter body length (Sachs et al. 2013).","Despite early historical depictions of snake-like coils, the neck was constrained by interlocking zygapophyses and massive lateral ligaments that restricted vertical flexion while allowing gentle horizontal sweeps.","Long, needle-like, interlocking teeth projected outward from the snout tips, forming an effective fish trap for snaring small shoaling teleost fish and cephalopods.","Gastric contents routinely preserve polished siliceous gastroliths (stomach stones), utilized to aid in grinding food and regulating hydrostatic buoyancy control.","All four limbs were modified into stiff, hydrofoil-shaped flippers powered by powerful pectoral and pelvic girdles in a four-winged underwater flight stroke."]
sizeNotes: Total length was 10.3 meters (34 feet), of which 7.1 meters was the neck. Note: Holotype ANSP 13183 with 71 preserved cervical vertebrae measures exactly 10.3 m total length (neck 7.1 m, trunk ~1.8 m, tail ~1.4 m). Torso depth 1.2 m, mass ~2,000 kg.

name: Giganotosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1993 by Rubén Darío Carolini in Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally named Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995 by Coria and Salgado.
• Additional fragments of a potentially larger individual were found in later years.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia, Giganotosaurus measured an estimated 12.2 to 13 meters in length, rivaling Tyrannosaurus in overall body length.","Its skull measured over 1.6 meters in length, armed with serrated, compressed teeth that functioned like butcher's blades to slice flesh and cause massive hemorrhaging.","Finite element analysis reveals high torsional and shearing resistance in its fused mandibular symphysis, built to withstand violent lateral jerking against giant sauropods.","Histological analysis of the holotype femur indicates that Giganotosaurus attained adult size within approximately 15 to 20 years, experiencing explosive growth rates."]
sizeNotes: Very large. Note: Holotype MUCPv-Ch1 is 12.2–12.5 m (representative 12.5 m), standing hip height 3.9 m, mass 7,000–8,500 kg (representative 7,500 kg). 13.2 m represents the fragmentary max jaw MUCPv-95.

name: Deinonychus
dietDetails: Pack hunter
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1931 by Barnum Brown in Montana.
• John Ostrom redefined our understanding of dinosaurs by describing it in 1969.
• Ostrom's study of Deinonychus sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance'.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by John Ostrom in 1964 in the Cloverly Formation of Montana, Deinonychus sparked the modern 'Dinosaur Renaissance' by proving dinosaurs were active, warm-blooded animals.","Possessed a hyper-extensible second toe armed with a 12-centimeter recurved sickle claw (falciform ungual), used for pinning prey and gripping flesh while climbing.","Its stiffened tail was reinforced by hyper-elongated vertebral prezygapophyses and ossified chevrons, acting as a dynamic gyroscopic counterbalance during high-speed leaps.","Direct associations with the ornithopod Tenontosaurus in multiple quarries provide compelling evidence of coordinated pack hunting or aggressive gregarious feeding."]
sizeNotes: Agile.

name: Albertosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1884 by Joseph Burr Tyrrell in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Albertosaurus in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn.
• A massive bonebed containing over 20 individuals was found in 1910.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, by Joseph B. Tyrrell in 1884, serving as the foundational genus of Albertosaurinae.","The famous Dry Island Buffalo Jump bonebed yielded at least 26 distinct individuals, offering unprecedented statistical evidence of pack living and gregarious social hierarchy.","Possessed longer, more gracile hindlimbs than Tyrannosaurus, with an arctometatarsalian foot structure that made it a faster, more cursorial pursuer of hadrosaurs.","Cranial scans reveal well-developed olfactory bulbs and acute stereoscopic vision, optimized for coordinated pursuit hunting across open Late Cretaceous floodplains."]

name: Utahraptor
dietDetails: Large prey
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1991 by a team led by James Kirkland in Utah.
• Officially named Utahraptor ostrommaysi in 1993.
• Additional specimens have since been found trapped in a potential quicksand predator trap.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, measuring roughly 5 to 7 meters in length and weighing over 300 to 500 kilograms.","Represents the largest known dromaeosaurid dinosaur, possessing a massive, 24-centimeter sickle claw on its second pedal digit supported by robust, stocky hindlimbs.","Unlike gracile dromaeosaurs that relied on high-speed cursorial sprinting, Utahraptor was an ambush bruiser with thickened bones built for wrestling large iguanodonts.","A colossal 9-metric-ton fossil 'quicksand block' excavated in Utah contains an adult and multiple juvenile Utahraptors preserved together alongside iguanodont prey."]
sizeNotes: Heavy build. Note: Stored 7.0m was an early popular estimate. The adult holotype and associated specimens establish length of 5.5–6.0 m (representative 5.7 m), hip height 1.6 m, mass ~450–600 kg (representative 500 kg).

name: Oviraptor
dietDetails: Opportunist
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1923 by George Olsen during an expedition to Mongolia.
• Named 'egg thief' because the first fossil was found atop a clutch of eggs.
• Later discoveries proved the eggs belonged to Oviraptor itself, and it was brooding them.
interestingFacts: ["Originally discovered in 1924 atop a nest of fossilized eggs and named 'egg thief' under the mistaken assumption it was stealing Protoceratops eggs.","Excavations in the 1990s revealed an oviraptorid embryo preserved inside an identical egg, proving the animal died while faithfully brooding its own clutch.","Its skull was short, deep, and completely toothless, equipped with a powerful keratinous beak powered by hypertrophied jaw adductor muscles to crack tough seeds and shells.","Possessed a highly pneumatic skull roof and an avian-style furcula (wishbone), illustrating the intimate evolutionary kinship between maniraptorans and birds."]
sizeNotes: Parrot-like beak. Note: Holotype AMNH 6517 confirms total body length ~1.6 m, standing hip height 0.7 m (1.0m was an overextended upright neck pose), mass ~35 kg.

name: Majungasaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1896 by a French military officer in Madagascar.
• Originally named Megalosaurus crenatissimus by Charles Depéret in 1896.
• A complete skull discovered in 1996 clarified its classification as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["The undisputed apex predator of Late Cretaceous Madagascar's Maevarano Formation, measuring roughly 6 to 7 meters in body length.","Bone surfaces belonging to Majungasaurus frequently bear distinctive theropod feeding tooth marks with inter-denticle spacing matching only Majungasaurus itself, confirming cannibalism.","Possessed a single, rounded bony horn projecting from the fused frontal bones of its skull roof, likely used for ritualized intra-specific head-butting.","Its forelimbs were reduced to tiny, non-functional four-fingered stumps that lacked distinct wrist bones and could not flex at the elbow."]
sizeNotes: Top predator of Madagascar.

name: Baryonyx
dietDetails: Piscivore
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1983 by amateur fossil hunter William Walker in Surrey, England.
• Described in 1986 by Alan Charig and Angela Milner.
• The holotype specimen included fish scales in its stomach region.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1983 by amateur collector William Walker in Surrey, England, within the Early Cretaceous Weald Clay Formation.","Possessed a massive, 31-centimeter curved claw on its first manual digit (thumb), which it used to gaff fish from river currents like a modern grizzly bear.","Its elongated, gavial-like snout bore a spoon-shaped terminal rosette lined with 96 finely serrated, sub-conical teeth tailored for gripping slippery fish.","Fossilized stomach contents preserved the acid-etched scales and bones of the Cretaceous teleost fish Lepidotes alongside partially digested juvenile Iguanodon bones."]
sizeNotes: Fish eater. Note: Holotype BMNH R9951 measures 7.5–8.5 m (representative 8.5 m), standing hip height 2.3 m. Stored mass of 1,200 kg was an underestimate; volumetric regressions place adult mass at 1,700–2,000 kg (representative 1,800 kg).

name: Acrocanthosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the early 1940s in Oklahoma, USA.
• Named Acrocanthosaurus atokensis in 1950 by Stovall and Langston.
• A nearly complete skeleton 'Fran' was discovered in the 1990s.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Early Cretaceous Antlers and Twin Mountains Formations of Oklahoma and Texas, reaching lengths of over 11.5 meters.","Characterized by hyper-elongated neural spines on its cervical, dorsal, and caudal vertebrae that rose up to 2.5 times the height of the vertebral centra.","These neural spines anchored an immense, thick muscular ridge or fleshy hump that stabilized the spine and distributed mechanical loads when tackling large sauropods.","The famed Paluxy River trackway in Texas preserves fossilized footprints widely attributed to an Acrocanthosaurus stalking a herd of sauropods across a tidal mudflat."]

name: Dromaeosaurus
dietDetails: Small prey
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1914 by Barnum Brown in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
• Named by Brown and Matthew in 1922.
• The type species of the family Dromaeosauridae.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by Barnum Brown in 1914 along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, serving as the type genus of the family Dromaeosauridae.","Possessed a remarkably short, deep skull that differed sharply from the slender, elongated snouts of contemporary dromaeosaurids like Saurornitholestes.","Biomechanical jaw simulations indicate Dromaeosaurus had a crushing bite force nearly three times greater than that of Velociraptor, capable of crushing bone.","Its teeth were stout, strongly recurved, and bore heavy chisel-like denticles that resisted severe bending stresses during violent biting."]
sizeNotes: Small but powerful. Note: Holotype AMNH 5356 and cranial-scaling confirm total length ~1.9 m, standing hip height 0.6 m, mass ~15–20 kg (representative 17 kg).

name: Troodon
dietDetails: Small prey
discoveryHistory:
• A single tooth was discovered in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden.
• Named by Joseph Leidy in 1856, making it one of the first dinosaurs named in North America.
• The genus has been considered a 'wastebasket taxon' due to confusing fossil fragments.
interestingFacts: ["Historically described by Joseph Leidy in 1856 based on a single serrated tooth, Troodon became the archetypal symbol of Mesozoic dinosaurian intelligence.","Possessed the highest encephalization quotient (brain-to-body mass ratio) of any non-avian dinosaur, with enlarged cerebrums and expansive optic lobes.","Its large, forward-facing orbits provided a high degree of binocular vision and stereoscopic depth perception for hunting small mammals and reptiles at twilight.","Recent taxonomic revisions have split classic 'Troodon' material into distinct genera (such as Stenonychosaurus and Latenivenatrix) due to subtle cranial and pelvic variations."]
sizeNotes: Intelligent.

name: Gorgosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
• Over 20 skeletons have been found, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids.
interestingFacts: ["A fleet-footed albertosaurine tyrannosaurid from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, known from dozens of complete skeletons.","Possessed long, slender metatarsals and a fused arctometatarsalian foot structure, making it one of the fastest cursorial apex predators of the Late Cretaceous.","A spectacular 2023 juvenile Gorgosaurus fossil was found with the articulated hind legs of two yearling caenagnathid dinosaurs (Citipes) preserved in its stomach cavity.","This sensational stomach-content discovery provided direct physical proof that tyrannosaurids shifted dietary niches from fast small game as juveniles to giant ceratopsians as adults."]
sizeNotes: Fast runner.

name: Daspletosaurus
dietDetails: Apex predator
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles Mortram Sternberg in Alberta.
• Dale Russell recognized it as a distinct genus and named it in 1970.
• Some specimens show bite marks from other tyrannosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["A massive, robust tyrannosaurine from Alberta, Canada, that lived alongside the more gracile and agile albertosaurine Gorgosaurus.","Possessed a heavily reinforced skull with thickened postorbital bones and robust ziphodont teeth capable of puncturing through thick ceratopsian bone and armor.","Fossil skulls frequently exhibit unhealed and healed bite marks inflicted by other tyrannosaurs, documenting fierce intra-specific territorial battles and face-biting.","Endocranial reconstructions reveal an extraordinarily acute sense of smell, with massive olfactory tracts extending forward from the cerebral hemispheres."]
sizeNotes: Apex predator. Note: Holotype CMN 8506 is 9.0 m long, hip height 2.9 m. Heavy, robust build exceeds *Gorgosaurus*; adult mass is ~2,800–3,500 kg (representative 3,000 kg).

name: Styracosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was collected in 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg in Alberta.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
• Bonebeds suggest it lived in massive herds.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, characterized by one of the most spectacular cranial ornamentations in Dinosauria.","Its parietosquamosal frill bore four to six long, sharp, backward-projecting spikes measuring up to 60 centimeters in length.","The nasal bone was crowned with a massive, straight nose horn that reached nearly 60 centimeters in length and was sheathed in tough keratin.","Enormous monospecific bonebeds containing hundreds of individuals indicate that Styracosaurus lived and migrated in massive, socially coordinated herds."]
sizeNotes: Spectacular frill.

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1946 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Described and named in 1950.
• The Pipestone Creek bonebed revealed hundreds of individuals.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Pipestone Creek bonebed in Alberta, Canada, where thousands of disarticulated bones representing dozens of individuals were recovered.","Instead of a sharp nasal horn, Pachyrhinosaurus bore an enormous, flattened, rugose bony mass known as a nasal boss, which supported a thick keratinous battering ram.","Its frill featured a pair of curved, forward-pointing hook-like spikes on the upper midline and a small, horn-like unicorn spike in the center of the forehead.","Microscopic bone histology suggests that the cranial boss was highly vascularized and actively remodeled during sexual maturity for display and flank-butting."]
sizeNotes: Herd animal.

name: Centrosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Lawrence Lambe in 1904 in Alberta, Canada.
• Lambe named the genus that same year based on incomplete remains.
• Enormous bonebeds in Dinosaur Provincial Park have yielded thousands of bones.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most common ceratopsians recovered from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, known from dense bonebeds containing thousands of specimens.","Possessed a single, large nasal horn that curved forward or backward depending on maturity and individual variation, paired with forward-curving hooks on its frill.","Its deep, robust jaws housed continuous shearing dental batteries consisting of hundreds of interlocking teeth that replaced worn crowns continuously.","The massive Hildegard bonebed preserves an entire herd of Centrosaurus that drowned simultaneously while attempting to cross a swollen, flooding tropical river."]
sizeNotes: Single large nasal horn.

name: Chasmosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• First remains found in 1898 by Lawrence Lambe.
• Formally named by Lambe in 1914.
• Multiple species have been identified from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, distinguished by an extraordinarily expansive, heart-shaped neck frill.","Its parietal-squamosal frill accounted for nearly half the total skull length, perforated by enormous fenestrae (openings) that lightened its display surface.","Spectacular fossil specimens preserve pristine skin impressions displaying a mosaic of large, multi-faceted polygon scales bordered by smaller circular scales.","Possessed a relatively short nasal horn and two small brow horns, relying primarily on its brightly colored, vascularized frill for intra-specific signaling."]
sizeNotes: Elongated frill.

name: Psittacosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1922 by the American Museum of Natural History expedition to Mongolia.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• Hundreds of complete skeletons have been found, making it one of the most studied dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most abundant and well-studied dinosaurs in the fossil record, with over 1,000 articulated skeletons excavated from Cretaceous beds of East Asia.","Possessed an upright, obligate bipedal stance and a parrot-like crushing beak powered by deep cheek muscles to break open tough seeds and nuts.","A world-famous fossil specimen from Liaoning, China, preserves a dense brush of long, stiff, tubular bristles (integumentary appendages) running down the top of its tail.","Spectacular ultraviolet and laser-stimulated fluorescence imaging revealed fossilized countershading camouflage, with a dark dorsal surface and pale ventral belly."]
sizeNotes: Bipedal.

name: Pentaceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles H. Sternberg in the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• A massive skull was discovered in 1941, one of the largest of any terrestrial animal.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Kirtland Formation of the San Juan Basin in New Mexico, measuring roughly 6 to 7 meters in total length.","Its name means 'five-horned face', referencing its prominent nose horn, two forward-curving brow horns, and two sharply flared jugal cheek spikes.","Possessed one of the largest skulls of any land animal, with an immense, rectangular neck frill that reached nearly 2.3 to 3 meters in total vertical height.","Its broad frill bore small, scalloped osteoderms (epoccipitals) along the margin, serving as an intimidating visual billboard to rivals and predators."]
sizeNotes: Prominent cheek horns.

name: Diabloceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was found in 2002 by Don DeBlieux in Utah's Wahweap Formation.
• Described and named by James Kirkland and colleagues in 2010.
• Represents one of the oldest known centrosaurine ceratopsids.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Wahweap Formation of Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, dating to ~79 million years ago.","One of the most basal known centrosaurines, distinguished by a pair of long, curved, devil-like spikes rising upward from the top of its neck frill.","Possessed unusually long, slender supraorbital (brow) horns for a centrosaurine, retaining the primitive horn configuration seen in basal chasmosaurines.","Its deep snout was equipped with a sharp, keratinous cropping beak, adapted for browsing tough, woody riparian shrubs and palm fronds."]
sizeNotes: Basal centrosaurine. Note: Stored 5.5m was an overestimate. Complete holotype UMNH VP 16699 indicates adult length of 4.2–4.8 m (representative 4.5 m), hip height 1.6 m, mass ~1,300–1,600 kg (representative 1,400 kg).

name: Kosmoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 2006 by a volunteer in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Formally named by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
• Its discovery shed light on dinosaur endemism in Late Cretaceous North America.
interestingFacts: ["The most decorated and ornate ceratopsian dinosaur ever discovered, bearing an extraordinary total of 15 individual horns and horn-like processes across its skull—more cranial weaponry and display structures than any other known non-avian dinosaur.","Its 15 cranial horns break down with morphological precision: 1 blade-like nasal horn above the snout, 2 pointed postorbital brow horns curving outward over the eyes, 2 laterally projecting jugal (cheek) horns, and exactly 10 distinct epioccipital and epiparietal horns ringing the dorsal margin of its parietal frill.","Eight of the 10 frill horns curve dramatically forward and downward over the forehead like an elaborate decorative fringe of bangs, while the outermost two curve laterally, an anatomical orientation useless for combat but exquisitely evolved for visual socio-sexual display.","Discovered in 2006 by volunteer Scott Richardson in the Kaiparowits Formation of southern Utah, living on the isolated greenhouse island continent of Laramidia approximately 76 million years ago."]
sizeNotes: Most ornate skull.

name: Zuniceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 by eight-year-old Christopher James Wolfe in New Mexico.
• Described and named by Douglas Wolfe and James Kirkland in 1998.
• Provides a crucial evolutionary link between earlier ceratopsians and later giants.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Moreno Hill Formation of Catron County, New Mexico, by eight-year-old Christopher Wolfe in 1998.","Represents the earliest known North American ceratopsian to possess prominent supraorbital (brow) horns, living roughly 91 million years ago.","Morphologically bridges the evolutionary gap between small Asian ceratopsians (like Protoceratops) and the colossal multi-ton Ceratopsidae.","Fossil bonebeds indicate that Zuniceratops lived in family groups that grazed along coastal floodplain swamps bordering the Western Interior Seaway."]
sizeNotes: Small and early.

name: Sinoceratops
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 in the Shandong province of China.
• Described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues in 2010.
• The first ceratopsid dinosaur ever found outside of North America.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Xingezhuang Formation of Shandong Province, China, representing the first definitive ceratopsid dinosaur discovered outside North America.","A basal centrosaurine measuring roughly 6 meters in length and weighing over 2 metric tons, with an immensely thickened nasal horn base.","Its parietosquamosal frill featured a distinct row of forward-curving, horn-like epiparietal hooks running across the top margin.","Its discovery proved that advanced ceratopsids migrated across the Beringian land bridge and successfully colonized Late Cretaceous Asian ecosystems."]
sizeNotes: Unique frill.

name: Einiosaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1985 by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995.
• Found in low-diversity bonebeds, indicating it lived in herds.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, celebrated for its unique, forward-curving, hook-like nasal horn.","The nasal horn curved strongly downward and forward over the front of the beak, functioning as a ritualized wrestling hook rather than an impaling weapon.","Its parietosquamosal frill bore a pair of large, backward-pointing spikes (epiparietals) that projected straight from the top corners.","Represents a key intermediate transitional evolutionary stage linking primitive centrosaurines like Centrosaurus to derived forms like Achelousaurus."]
sizeNotes: Herd dweller.

name: Achelousaurus
dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner in Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995 alongside Einiosaurus.
• Represents an evolutionary transition between Einiosaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Upper Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana, named in honor of paleontologist Jack Horner.","Lacked true pointed horns, possessing instead heavily rugose, flattened bony pads (bosses) over both the snout and orbital regions.","Its neck frill retained two prominent, straight, backward-directed spikes extending from the posterior parietal margin.","Represents an exquisite example of anagenesis (lineage evolution without branching), directly descended from Einiosaurus and ancestral to Pachyrhinosaurus."]

dietDetails: Low browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Described by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2013.
• Added to the growing list of unique dinosaurs from the region.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Kaiparowits Formation of southern Utah, dating to the late Campanian (~75.5 million years ago).","Possessed extraordinarily long, forward-curving brow horns that extended almost horizontally over its snout, resembling modern cattle.","Its snout was exceptionally deep and round, with an enlarged pneumatic nasal cavity that comprised over 75% of total pre-orbital skull length.","Its short, round neck frill lacked large spikes, relying instead on its bull-like horns and deep snout profile for visual display and sparring."]

name: Edmontosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• First remains were found in the late 19th century during the Bone Wars.
• Lawrence Lambe named the genus Edmontosaurus in 1917.
• Some of the best-preserved dinosaur mummies belong to this genus.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest hadrosaurids, reaching lengths of up to 12 to 15 meters and an estimated weight exceeding 9 metric tons.","Sensational 'mummy' specimens (such as AMNH 5060 and 'Dakota') preserve fossilized skin, muscle envelopes, hoof-like keratinous forefoot mitts, and soft-tissue fleshy combs atop the head.","Housed a continuous dental battery containing over 1,000 tightly interlocking teeth that operated as an efficient grinding mill for tough conifer needles and twigs.","Taphonomic evidence demonstrates that giant packs of Edmontosaurus formed the primary prey base for adult Tyrannosaurus rex across western North America."]
sizeNotes: Very common.

interestingFacts: ["Discovered along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, within the Dinosaur Park Formation, named for its helmet-like cranial crest.","Its hollow, semi-circular crest was formed from expanded nasal and premaxillary bones, housing convoluted internal acoustic air passages.","Acoustic modeling indicates the crest functioned as a low-frequency resonating chamber capable of broadcasting foghorn-like vocalizations over long distances.","Several fully articulated specimens preserve extensive impressions of tuberculate skin with polygonal scales covering the flanks and tail."]

name: Maiasaura
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1978 by Marion Brandvold in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Jack Horner and Robert Makela named it Maiasaura in 1979.
• 'Egg Mountain' yielded nests, eggs, embryos, and juveniles.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, Maiasaura translates to 'good mother lizard'.","Excavations at 'Egg Mountain' uncovered colonial nesting grounds, fossilized egg clutches, and nests containing altricial hatchlings with worn teeth.","The presence of worn teeth in nestling hatchlings provided the first definitive proof that dinosaurs actively brought food to their young and engaged in prolonged parental care.","Dense bonebeds containing an estimated 10,000 individuals indicate that Maiasaura traveled in colossal herds that migrated seasonally across coastal plains."]

name: Tsintaosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1950 in Shandong Province, China.
• C.C. Young named the genus in 1958.
• Its distinctive crest was initially thought to be an artifact of preservation.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Jingangkou Formation of Shandong Province, China, dating to the late Campanian stage (~72 Ma).","Famous for its iconic tubular cranial crest: once thought to be a unicorn-like spike, comprehensive re-examinations confirmed it formed the posterior wall of a broad hollow crest.","The hollow crest was connected directly to the nasal cavity and functioned in species recognition, olfactory enhancement, and vocal resonance.","Possessed robust, quadrupedal forelimbs and a heavy pelvic girdle, allowing it to transition effortlessly between four-legged browsing and bipedal running."]

name: Lambeosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• First materials collected in 1902 by Lawrence Lambe.
• William Parks named it Lambeosaurus in 1923 in honor of Lambe.
• Has had a complicated taxonomic history with many species consolidated over time.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, serving as the foundational type genus of the subfamily Lambeosaurinae.","Possessed a distinctive hatchet-shaped cranial crest comprising a vertical anterior blade and a slender, backward-pointing posterior horn.","Exhibited pronounced sexual and ontogenetic dimorphism: adult males possessed significantly larger, more upright crests than females and juveniles.","Its tail was deep and stiffened by a crisscrossing lattice of ossified tendons, providing balance while galloping or wading across coastal floodplains."]

name: Ouranosaurus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1965 by French paleontologist Philippe Taquet in Niger.
• Formally described and named in 1976.
• Found in the same geological formation as Spinosaurus.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Elrhaz Formation of Niger, dating to the Early Cretaceous (Aptian stage, ~112 million years ago).","Its dorsal vertebrae bore hyper-elongated, blade-like neural spines up to 1 meter tall, forming a high dorsal sail or thick muscular fat-storage hump.","Possessed a wide, flattened, duck-like bill followed by specialized dental batteries, optimized for harvesting tough riparian ferns, horsetails, and shrubs.","Retained a small, conical thumb spike on its first manual digit, utilized for defense against contemporary apex theropods like Suchomimus."]

name: Saurolophus
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1911 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named in 1912 by Brown.

interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, with a closely related giant sister species (S. angustirostris) excavated in the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia.","Possessed a solid, backward-pointing, rod-like cranial crest constructed from the nasal bones that projected over the top of the skull roof.","Pristine skin impressions demonstrate that Saurolophus bore distinct vertical stripes of large, raised limpet-shaped scales along its tail and flanks.","Proves that late hadrosaurine lineages migrated freely between East Asia and North America across the Cretaceous Beringian land bridge."]

name: Olorotitan
dietDetails: Browser
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 in the Amur Region of Far Eastern Russia.
• Named in 2003 by Pascal Godefroit and colleagues.
• Its skeleton was exceptionally complete for an Asian hadrosaur.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in the Tsagayan Formation of the Amur Region in far eastern Russia, dating to the latest Maastrichtian (~66 Ma).","Characterized by a unique, backward-pointing, fan-shaped cranial crest that rose vertically from the back of the skull like an inverted ax blade.","Possessed an exceptionally elongated neck comprising 18 cervical vertebrae, more than any other known hadrosaur, providing broad vertical browse reach.","Its sacrum and proximal caudal vertebrae were reinforced by additional fused bony bridges, supporting a massive body mass near the K-Pg boundary."]

name: Rajasaurus narmadensis
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large titanosaurian sauropods and ornithopods in Cretaceous floodplains.
discoveryHistory:
• Unearthed between 1981 and 1983 by Geological Survey of India (GSI) geologists G.N. Dwivedi and Dhananjay Mohabey near Rahioli, Gujarat.
• Excavated under the leadership of GSI paleontologist Suresh Srivastava, who recovered a nearly complete braincase and associated skeleton.
• Formally described in 2003 by a joint Indian-American team including Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson after two decades in storage.
• Designated as the holotype GSI Type No. 19/999, providing crucial evidence of abelisaurid distribution on southern landmasses.
interestingFacts: ["Discovered in 1983 by Suresh Srivastava in the Lameta Formation of Gujarat, western India, along the banks of the Narmada River; its name means 'princely lizard of Narmada'.","Possessed a prominent, rounded horn core on the midline of its skull roof formed by the fused frontal bones, utilized for intra-specific head-butting.","A formidable abelisaurid measuring roughly 7.5 to 9 meters in length, acting as the undisputed apex macropredator of the isolated Late Cretaceous Indian subcontinent.","Preyed upon the diverse titanosaurian sauropods (such as Jainosaurus and Isisaurus) that nested in immense numbers along the volcanic floodplains of the Deccan Traps."]
sizeNotes: Consensus length of 6.6 to 7.4 meters and weight of 1.5 metric tonnes, standing about 2.4 meters tall at the hip. Note: Holotype GSI 21141/1–33 confirms adult length of 6.6–7.0 m (representative 6.8 m), standing hip height 2.2 m, mass ~1,500 kg.

name: Indosuchus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator of small to medium-sized dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Collected between 1917 and 1919 by British geologist Charles Alfred Matley near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh.
• Formally named by German paleontologist Friedrich von Huene in 1932.
• Described in detail by Huene and Matley in a joint monograph in 1933.
• Originally classified as an allosaurid, then a tyrannosaurid, before modern analysis confirmed it as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: ["Excavated from the Late Cretaceous Lameta Formation of Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, India, by Charles Alfred Matley and described by Friedrich von Huene in 1933.","Possessed a remarkably narrow, laterally compressed skull with deep alveolar margins, specialized for delivering high-velocity slicing bites against tough sauropod hide.","Historically classified as a carnosaur or tyrannosauroid, modern cladistic analyses place Indosuchus firmly within Abelisauridae alongside Rajasaurus.","Its discovery proved that abelisaurid theropods achieved immense ecological and morphological diversity across Gondwanan landmasses before the K-Pg extinction."]
sizeNotes: Estimated to be roughly 6 to 7 meters in length and weighing 1.2 metric tonnes.

name: Irritator challengeri
nameMeaning: Irritating one, named after Professor Challenger
dietDetails: Piscivorous specialist snatching fish, pterosaurs, and small aquatic reptiles with snappy jaws.
discoveryHistory:
• Skull acquired from illegal fossil dealers who had artificial plaster added to make it look complete.
• Described in 1996 by Martill, Cruickshank, Frey, Small, and Clarke; named 'Irritator' due to the frustration of removing fake plaster.
• Species name honors Professor Challenger from Arthur Conan Doyle's 'The Lost World'.
interestingFacts: ["Received its name because paleontologists were immensely irritated by fossil poachers vandalizing the skull with plaster.","A tooth belonging to Irritator was found embedded inside a fossilized pterosaur spine, confirming pterosaur predation.","Possessed an exceptionally fast jaw closure mechanism, lowering its lower jaw sideways to swallow fish whole.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate medium-sized spinosauridtheropod measuring approximately 7.5 meters long, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Medium-sized spinosauridtheropod measuring approximately 7.5 meters long.

name: Spinosaurus mirabilis
dietDetails: Large freshwater fishes including Mawsonia, Lepidotes, and lungfish.
discoveryHistory: Fossil material discovered in the Farak Formation of central Niger (localities Iguidi and Jenguebi) during expeditions in 2000, 2019, and 2022. Formally described by Paul Sereno and colleagues in February 2026 as the first new Spinosaurus species named in over a century.
interestingFacts: ["First new Spinosaurus species named in over a century, formally described in February 2026 by Paul Sereno and colleagues.","Possesses the tallest skull crest of any known theropod, featuring a dramatic scimitar-shaped cranial blade rising ~50 cm.","The cranial crest was covered in a keratinous sheath in life, likely serving as a colorful visual billboard for species and mate recognition.","Recovered from the fluvial Farak Formation in central Niger, providing conclusive proof that giant spinosaurids thrived in inland river systems.","Shared its ecosystem with large freshwater coelacanths (Mawsonia) and crocodylomorphs, utilizing its slender conical-toothed jaws to snatch aquatic prey."]
sizeNotes: Immature holotype indicates subadult growth; adult individuals are estimated to have reached ~12.0–13.0 m in length, ~3.8 m tall at the sail, and ~6,500 kg. Note: Sereno et al. (2026); subadult holotype extrapolated to adult length 12.5 m, sail height 3.8 m, mass 6,500 kg.

dietDetails: Opportunistic predator and scavenger feeding on fish, marine reptiles, and floating dinosaur carcasses.

discoveryHistory:
• First described by Louis Agassiz in 1843 from teeth found in Cretaceous marine strata.
• Fossilized teeth are extremely common across North American and European Cretaceous marine deposits.
• In 2010, a specimen was discovered with fossilized bones of a mosasaur inside its stomach region.
interestingFacts: ["Known as the 'Crow Shark' due to its ubiquitous presence as a scavenger in Cretaceous seas.","Fossilized Squalicorax teeth have been found embedded in the bones of terrestrial dinosaurs, proving it scavenged on carcasses washed out to sea.","Possessed distinctive serrated, crescent-shaped teeth perfect for slicing through tough flesh and bone.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate average length between 2 to 5 meters, with serrated teeth specialized for cutting, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Average length between 2 to 5 meters, with serrated teeth specialized for cutting.

name: Zalmoxes robustus
nameMeaning: Named after Zalmoxis, a Dacian deity
dietDetails: Low-level browser feeding on ferns, horsetails, and flowering plants on Hațeg Island.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Baron Franz Nopcsa in 1900 under the genus Mochlodon.
• Reclassified as the distinct genus Zalmoxes by Weishampel et al. in 2003.
• Nopcsa used Zalmoxes fossils to formulate his pioneering theory of insular dwarfism in dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: ["Lived on Hațeg Island, an isolated landmass in Late Cretaceous Europe, leading to insular dwarfism.","Possessed a surprisingly robust, heavy skull compared to its small overall body size.","Served as a primary herbivorous prey species for the giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate classic example of insular dwarfism; significantly smaller than mainland iguanodontians, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Classic example of insular dwarfism; significantly smaller than mainland iguanodontians.

dietDetails: Apex predator using giant hand claws to capture and disembowel ornithopod and sauropod prey.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1998 by Fernando Novas in Neuquén Province, Argentina.
• Initially mistaken for a giant dromaeosaurid due to an enormous claw assumed to belong to the foot.
• 2004 discovery of complete forelimbs revealed the massive sickle claw actually belonged to the hand (Digit I).

dietDetails: Apex superpredator preying upon titanosaurs and ornithopods in latest Cretaceous Patagonia.
discoveryHistory:

name: Lythronax argestes
dietDetails: Apex predator utilizing wide binocular vision and crushing bite force to hunt ceratopsids and hadrosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2009 in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, Utah.
• Formally described in 2013 by Mark Loewen and colleagues.
• Holotype specimen UMNH VP 20200 includes skull, postcranial elements, and gastralia.
interestingFacts: ["Nickname 'Gore King' comes from its scientific name translating directly to 'King of Gore'.","Possessed broad skull rear and narrow snout, giving it overlapping 3D binocular vision like T. rex 13 million years earlier.","Proved that tyrannosaurid radiation occurred much earlier than previously assumed.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate estimated at 8 meters in length and 2.5 tonnes; earliest true tyrannosaurid known, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

• Formally described in Communications Biology in February 2019.
• Represents the earliest diagnostic Cretaceous tyrannosauroid in North America.

name: Sauroposeidon proteles
nameMeaning: Lizard god of earthquakes, perfected before the end
dietDetails: High-canopy browser feeding on tall conifers, cycads, and ginkgos up to 18 meters above ground.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Gulf Coast / Interior Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Antlers Formation, Cloverly Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• Four massive neck vertebrae discovered in Oklahoma in 1994 by prison trainer Bobby Cross.
• Initially stored as petrified wood for five years before paleontologists recognized their true nature.
• Formally described in 2000 by Mathew Wedel, Richard Cifelli, and Kent Sanders.
interestingFacts: ["Its neck reached up to 12 meters (39 feet) in length, accounting for over one-third of its total body length.","Cervical vertebrae were up to 1.4 meters long and filled with honeycombed internal air cells (trabecular bone).","Stood as tall as a 6-story building, allowing it to browse vegetation inaccessible to any other creature.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate stood up to 18 meters (60 feet) high, making it one of the tallest land animals to ever live, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Stood up to 18 meters (60 feet) high, making it one of the tallest land animals to ever live.

name: Gillicus
dietDetails: Filter-feeding teleost fish scooping up small fish and zooplankton in open sea waters.

name: Yutyrannus huali
dietDetails: Apex predator of cool, temperate Early Cretaceous forests, hunting sauropods and iguanodontians.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by local fossil collectors in Liaoning Province, China, and acquired by Xu Xing.
• Formally described in Nature in April 2012 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Three nearly complete skeletons of varying ages preserved extensive filamentous plumage.

sizeNotes: Largest known dinosaur with direct, fossilized evidence of feathers. Note: Xu et al. (2012); holotype length 9.0 m, hip height 2.5 m, mass 1,400 kg.

name: Nanotyrannus lancensis
dietDetails: Fast, highly active predator hunting agile prey such as ornithomimids, pachycephalosaurs, and young dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Skull discovered in 1942 by Charles W. Gilmore and initially named Gorgosaurus lancensis.
• Renamed Nanotyrannus by Robert Bakker, Michael Williams, and Philip Currie in 1988.
• Long debated whether it is a valid distinct genus or a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex; 2024 studies by Longrich & Saitta reignited support for its validity.
interestingFacts: ["Subject of one of the longest and most fiercely contested debates in paleontology history.","Had significantly more teeth (up to 36 in upper jaw) and larger forelimbs than adult T. rex.","Possessed extremely long, slender leg bones adapted for high-speed pursuit running.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate slender, long-limbed theropod measuring roughly 5 meters in length and weighing ~900 kg, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Pyroraptor olympius
dietDetails: Agile, feathered pack hunter preying upon dwarf titanosaurs and iguanodontians on European islands.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1992 following a forest fire at Mount Olympe near Trets, Provence, France.
• Formally described in 2000 by Ronan Allain and Philippe Taquet.
• Remains include distinctive sickle toe claws, teeth, limb bones, and vertebrae.
interestingFacts: ["Named 'Fire Thief' because its fossils were uncovered immediately after a major forest fire.","Possessed a curved 6.5 cm sickle claw on the second toe of each foot for gripping prey.","Fully covered in feathers with wing-like plumage along its forelimbs.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate small dromaeosaurid dinosaur measuring 1.6 meters long and standing knee-high, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Small dromaeosaurid dinosaur measuring 1.6 meters long and standing knee-high.

name: Animantarx ramaljonesi
dietDetails: Low-level herbivore feeding on ferns, cycads, and low shrub vegetation.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 using radiological survey equipment by Ramal Jones.
• Formally described by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Donald Burge, and John Bird in 1999.
• Discovered specifically due to radioactive signals emitted by fossilized bones.
interestingFacts: ["First dinosaur discovered exclusively via radiological radiation detection technology.","Possessed a heavily armored skull with small horn-like projections behind the eyes.","Lacked a tail club, relying instead on shoulder spikes and fused armor plates.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate small nodosaurid ankylosaur measuring approximately 3 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Small nodosaurid ankylosaur measuring approximately 3 meters.

name: Segnosaurus galbinensis
dietDetails: Herbivorous theropod using long claws to hook branches and pluck leaves.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1973 in the Gobi Desert by Altangerel Perle.
• Formally described by Perle in 1979.
• Name-giver of the Segnosauria (now Therizinosauria) group.
interestingFacts: ["Bizarre theropod that evolved away from meat-eating to become a strict herbivore.","Possessed a massive pot belly to ferment tough plant vegetation.","Equipped with elongated, curved hand claws used to pull down tree branches.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate large therizinosaurid measuring 6 meters in length and weighing over 1 tonne, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Bajadasaurus pronuspinax
dietDetails: Low-level browser feeding on ferns, horsetails, and low vegetation using forward spines as defense.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2013 in Neuquén Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally described in Scientific Reports in 2019 by Pablo Gallina and colleagues.
• Preserved skull, neck vertebrae, and spectacular elongated neural spines.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed extremely long, thin neural spines along its neck that curved forward over its head.","The neck spines were likely covered in keratin sheaths, acting as defensive spikes against predators while grazing.","Eyes were positioned high on its skull, allowing it to look out for predators while lowering its snout to eat.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate dicraeosaurid sauropod measuring 9 meters long with dramatic forward-pointing neck spines, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Dicraeosaurid sauropod measuring 9 meters long with dramatic forward-pointing neck spines.

name: Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis
dietDetails: Medium-sized carnivore preying on ornithopods and sauropods in Early Cretaceous Japan.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 at the Kitadani Quarry in Katsuyama, Fukui Prefecture, Japan.
• Formally described in 2000 by Yoichi Azuma and Philip J. Currie.
• One of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Japan.
interestingFacts: ["Initially thought to be a dromaeosaurid due to a large hand claw, later recognized as a megaraptoran.","The state dinosaur mascot of Fukui Prefecture, Japan.","Possessed large hand claws used to grasp prey.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate medium-sized megaraptoran theropod reaching 4.2 meters in length, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Fukuisaurus tetoriensis
dietDetails: Herbivorous iguanodontian browsing on horsetails, ferns, and early flowering plants.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 alongside Fukuiraptor in Katsuyama, Fukui, Japan.
• Described in 2003 by Yoichi Azuma and Pascal Godefroit.
• Preserved skull and jaw material showing unique kinetic chewing adaptations.
interestingFacts: ["Skull lacked the kinetic flexibility seen in advanced hadrosaurs, chewing with a rigid maxilla.","Coexisted with Fukuiraptor, Fukuititan, and Koshisaurus in Early Cretaceous Japan.","Equipped with a sharp beak for clipping tough vegetation.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate bipedal/quadrupedal iguanodontian measuring 4.7 meters long, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Suchomimus tenerensis
dietDetails: Semiaquatic predator snatching giant fish (Mawsonia) and young dinosaurs from Cretaceous rivers.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 in the Ténéré Desert of Niger by team led by Paul Sereno.
• Formally described in Science in November 1998.
• Skeleton roughly 70% complete including skull, arms, claws, and vertebrae.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a narrow 1.2-meter long crocodile-like skull lined with 100 conical teeth.","Had a massive 30 cm sickle claw on its thumb used to spear fish.","Featured a low neural spine sail reaching up to 60 cm high along its back.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate large spinosaurid theropod measuring 11 meters in length and weighing nearly 4 tonnes, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Large spinosaurid theropod measuring 11 meters in length and weighing nearly 4 tonnes. Note: Sereno et al. (1998), Paul (2010); subadult holotype length 11.0 m, mass 3,800 kg.

name: Tropaeognathus mesembrinus
dietDetails: Ocean-going aerial piscivore skimming fish from the water surface using crested jaws.
discoveryHistory:
• Described in 1987 by Peter Wellnhofer from fossils in the Romualdo Formation, Brazil.
• 2013 skeleton specimen MN 6594-V described by Kellner et al. confirmed massive 8.2m wingspan.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest pre-azhdarchid flying reptiles known, with an 8.2-meter wingspan.","Possessed large convex keel-like crests on the tips of both upper and lower jaws.","Crests acted as rudders to stabilize jaws while dipping into water at high speed to catch fish.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate giant anhanguerid pterosaur with a wingspan reaching 8.2 meters (27 feet), providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]
sizeNotes: Giant anhanguerid pterosaur with a wingspan reaching 8.2 meters (27 feet). Note: Wingspan 8.2 m noted. Quadrupedal body length ~2.5 m, height ~1.5 m, mass ~28 kg (Kellner et al. 2013).

name: Coloborhynchus clavirostris
dietDetails: Coastal pelagic piscivore catching slippery marine fish with forward-pointing teeth.
discoveryHistory:

interestingFacts: ["Featured a unique flattened front snout tip with teeth projecting forward at odd angles.","Equipped with a prominent crest along the front upper jaw.","Earliest recognized anhanguerid pterosaur in the European fossil record.","Skeletal and biomechanical reconstructions indicate pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of approximately 5 to 6 meters, providing key insights into its growth dynamics."]

name: Alioramus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator preying on small-to-medium dinosaurs, oviraptorosaurs, and juvenile ornithischians.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a Soviet-Mongolian paleontological expedition in the Gobi Desert in the early 1970s and formally described by Sergei Kurzanov in 1976.
interestingFacts: ["Distinguished by a prominent row of five bony crests or bumps along the bridge of its slender snout.","Possessed more teeth than any other tyrannosaurid (76 to 78 teeth), adapted for seizing smaller, agile prey.","Its slender proportions led researchers to suggest it occupied a distinct ecological niche compared to apex Tarbosaurus.","Histological analysis of Alioramus altai showed that even near-adult individuals maintained a long, gracile snout."]
sizeNotes: Based on subadult holotype PIN 3141/1, characterized by a slender gracile build and elongated skull. Note: Kurzanov (1976), Brusatte et al. (2012); subadult length 5.5 m, mass 500 kg.

dietDetails: Active carnivore preying on small mammals, lizards, frogs, and juvenile dinosaurs; also scavenged larger carcasses.

sizeNotes: Lightly built dromaeosaurid with exceptionally long, slender hindlimbs and large sickle claws on the second toes.

name: Deinocheirus
dietDetails: Bulk omnivore feeding on soft aquatic vegetation, water plants, freshwater fish, and small aquatic invertebrates.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in 1965 by Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska as giant mysterious arms; its bizarre complete body with duck-bill and dorsal sail was revealed in 2014 by Lee et al.
interestingFacts: ["Remained one of paleontology's greatest mysteries for nearly 50 years when only its gargantuan arms were known.","Featured a prominent sail-like hump along its back supported by tall neural spines and a fused pygostyle at the tail tip.","Fossilized stomach contents revealed fish scales alongside over 1,400 gastroliths used to grind tough plant matter.","Possessed a wide, toothless, duck-like bill ideal for scooping aquatic vegetation in Cretaceous wetlands."]
sizeNotes: The largest known ornithomimosaurian, sporting massive 2.4-meter arms ending in blunt, curved 20-centimeter claws.

name: Erlikosaurus
dietDetails: Herbivore consuming foliage, ferns, fruits, and soft Cretaceous vegetation.
discoveryHistory: Found during a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in 1972 at Bayshin Tsav and formally named by Altangerel Perle in 1980.
interestingFacts: ["Provides the primary anatomical blueprint for the entire Therizinosauridae group thanks to its intact 25-centimeter skull.","Possessed a keratinous beak at the tip of its snout accompanied by small, leaf-shaped serrated teeth for stripping leaves.","Digital endocranial reconstructions revealed well-developed sense organs for hearing, balance, and spatial coordination.","Had slender, curved claws on its forelimbs used to hook high branches and pull foliage toward its mouth."]
sizeNotes: Known from the only exceptionally preserved complete skull of any therizinosaurid found to date (holotype MPC-D 100/111).

name: Tyrannotitan
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon massive titanosaurian sauropods such as Patagotitan and Chubutisaurus.
discoveryHistory: Found on the 'La Juanita' farm in Chubut in 1999 and formally described by Fernando Novas and colleagues in 2005.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest known giant carcharodontosaurids, predating both Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus.","Unlike its later relatives, its teeth were less blade-like and bore wrinkly, undulating enamel surfaces adapted for crushing flesh.","Possessed extraordinarily short and stout arms, showing early evolutionary reduction in forelimb size among giganotosaurines.","Lived alongside giant titanosaur sauropods, which it attacked using slashing, wound-inflicting bites."]
sizeNotes: Massive carcharodontosaurid comparable in size to Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus, with heavily built dorsal vertebrae.

name: Thalassodromeus
dietDetails: Terrestrial and aerial predator hunting small vertebrates, fish, squids, and lizards.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in calcium carbonate concretions in northeastern Brazil and described in 2002 by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
interestingFacts: ["Sported one of the largest cranial crests known relative to its skull, laced with extensive blood vessel impressions for thermoregulation and display.","Originally hypothesized to skim-feed, biomechanical studies later proved its neck and jaw could not withstand water resistance forces.","Operated as a terrestrial predator similar to modern storks, stalking small prey on the ground.","Its toothless, scissor-like jaws converged to a sharp tip capable of delivering powerful stabbing and slicing bites."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 4.2 to 4.5 meters; skull length of 1.4 meters, with the cranial crest accounting for 75% of skull surface area. Note: Wingspan 4.5 m noted. Standing height 1.6 m, body length 1.8 m, mass 23 kg (Kellner & Campos 2002).

name: Infernodrakon
dietDetails: Carnivorous azhdarchoid stalking small dinosaurs, mammals, amphibians, and reptiles on Cretaceous floodplains.
discoveryHistory: Named and described based on holotype cervical and wing material recovered from the upper Hell Creek Formation of Montana.
interestingFacts: ["Coexisted directly with Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, and the colossal giant pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus.","Demonstrates that medium-sized pterosaurs thrived alongside giant azhdarchids until the chicxulub asteroid impact.","Possessed elongated neck vertebrae and robust forelimbs adapted for efficient four-legged terrestrial stalking.","Features uniquely slender spear-like rostral morphology suggesting quick striking at small agile prey."]
sizeNotes: Mid-sized azhdarchid with an estimated wingspan of approximately 4.5 to 5.0 meters. Note: Wingspan 4.8 m noted. Quadrupedal body length 2.5 m, standing height 2.2 m, mass 40 kg.

dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon giant hadrosaurids like Shantungosaurus and large ceratopsians like Sinoceratops.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2009 during quarry excavations in Zhucheng and named by David Hone and colleagues in 2011.
interestingFacts: ["Shares anatomical features with Tarbosaurus but differs in having a distinctive horizontal shelf on the maxilla.","Hunted the colossal hadrosaur Shantungosaurus, one of the largest non-sauropod dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.","Lived in a floodplain ecosystem characterized by catastrophic mass mortality events that preserved thousands of dinosaur bones.","Bore massive, bone-crushing jaws with deep rooted teeth designed to withstand extreme lateral biting forces."]
sizeNotes: One of the largest known tyrannosaurids, nearly matching Tyrannosaurus rex and Tarbosaurus in maxilla and dentary dimensions.

name: Zhejiangopterus
dietDetails: Terrestrial stalker feeding on small vertebrates, lizards, eggs, and invertebrates.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1986 in Linhai County by a local quarry worker and described in 1994 by Cai Zhengquan and Wei Feng.
interestingFacts: ["One of the most anatomically complete azhdarchid pterosaurs ever discovered, providing critical data on azhdarchid neck structure.","Lacked the exaggerated cranial crests seen in many other pterosaurs, featuring a low, elongate, crestless skull with a sharp beak.","Its long neck vertebrae lacked cervical ribs, making the neck stiff and held upright like a modern stork.","Biomechanical analysis indicates it spent extensive time walking quadrupedally on land, picking off prey in open woodlands."]
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 3.5 meters; known from multiple well-preserved complete skeletons including juvenile and adult specimens. Note: Wingspan 3.5 m noted. Quadrupedal body length 1.6 m, standing height 1.5 m, mass 17 kg (Witton 2013).

name: Thanatotheristes
nameMeaning: Reaper of death, honoring De Groots
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon early ceratopsians like Xenoceratops and hadrosauroids.
discoveryHistory: Found along the Bow River in Alberta in 2010 by local hikers John and Sandra De Groot, and described in 2020 by Jared Voris and colleagues.
interestingFacts: ["Nicknamed the 'Reaper of Death', it is the oldest named tyrannosaurid discovered in Canada, predating T. rex by about 12 million years.","Distinguished by a unique series of vertical ridges along the upper jaw margin (maxilla) in front of the eye socket.","Forms a distinct clade (Daspletosaurini) with Daspletosaurus, demonstrating that tyrannosaurids were ecologically partitioned into distinct lineages.","Deep, robust jaw construction indicates it delivered crushing bites to disable thick-skinned ceratopsian prey."]
sizeNotes: Oldest known tyrannosaurid from northern North America, with an adult skull measuring approximately 80 cm.

name: Gigantoraptor
dietDetails: Omnivore or herbivore consuming high foliage, seeds, tubers, and opportunistically small vertebrates with its robust beak.
discoveryHistory: Accidentally unearthed in 2005 in front of a film crew filming a Japanese documentary on sauropod fossils; named in 2007 by Xu Xing et al.
interestingFacts: ["Reached a colossal size comparable to tyrannosaurids while retaining the light, bird-like skeletal features and toothless beak of oviraptorosaurs.","Bone histology of the holotype (LH V0011) revealed it was an 11-year-old subadult that was still actively growing at the time of death.","Despite weighing two tonnes, it had proportionally long, slender hind legs, indicating it was one of the fastest runners of its size.","Preserved pennaceous feathers on related oviraptorosaurs confirm that Gigantoraptor possessed feathered forelimbs used for brooding or display."]
sizeNotes: By far the largest known oviraptorosaurian, growing nearly 35 times heavier than most other oviraptorosaurs. Note: Xu et al. (2007); subadult holotype length 8.0 m, height 3.5 m, mass 2,000 kg.

name: Rinchenia
dietDetails: Omnivore feeding on seeds, nuts, foliage, eggs, mollusks, and small vertebrates in Cretaceous river floodplains.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1984 in the Nemegt Basin; originally described by Rinchen Barsbold as Oviraptor mongoliensis, and placed in its own genus Rinchenia in 1997 by Halszka Osmólska.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a dramatically tall, bulbous casque-like skull crest made of delicate porous bone, resembling that of a modern cassowary.","The crest served primarily as a visual display structure for species recognition and sexual selection in the lush Nemegt environment.","Equipped with an exceptionally robust, short lower jaw and toothless keratinous beak capable of cracking hard plant seeds and shellfish.","Its fused tail vertebrae (pygostyle) supported a fan of plumage used in mating displays."]
sizeNotes: Known from holotype MPC-D 100/32A, featuring a remarkably tall, thin, dome-like cranial crest.

name: Linhenykus
dietDetails: Specialized insectivore using its single stout thumb claw to dig into subterranean ant and termite mounds.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2008 in red sandstone beds at Bayan Mandahu by Jonah Choiniere and Michael Pittman, and described in 2011 by Xu Xing et al.
interestingFacts: ["The only known non-avian dinosaur to possess just a single functional finger (a stout clawed thumb) on each forelimb.","The second and third fingers were entirely absent or reduced to vestigial specks of bone, representing the extreme endpoint of theropod arm reduction.","Like modern pangolins and anteaters, its hyper-specialized single claws were adapted for ripping into hardened insect nests.","Had long, gracile bird-like hind legs capable of rapid running across arid desert dunes."]
sizeNotes: Tiny alvarezsaurid weighing under half a kilogram, famous for having only one functional digit on each hand.

name: Stomatosuchus
dietDetails: Piscivore and filter feeder straining small fish, crustaceans, and plankton using an expandable pelican-like throat pouch.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1911 by Ernst Stromer in the Bahariya Oasis, Egypt, and described in 1925; tragically, the sole holotype skull was destroyed during an Allied bombing raid on Munich in 1944.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed an entirely toothless lower jaw paired with only tiny conical teeth in the upper jaw, unique among giant crocodylomorphs.","Believed to have possessed a massive, flexible gular throat pouch like a pelican to trap shoals of freshwater fish.","The only known fossil specimen was destroyed when the Alte Akademie museum in Munich was bombed during World War II.","Coexisted in North Africa's mangrove swamps with Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus."]
sizeNotes: Giant crocodile with a flattened, shovel-shaped skull nearly 2 meters long, featuring a completely toothless lower jaw.

name: Kariridraco
dietDetails: Frugivore and opportunistic omnivore feeding on gymnosperm fruits, seeds, and small vertebrates in coastal forests.
discoveryHistory: Named and described in 2021 by Gabriela Cerqueira and colleagues from a well-preserved skull excavated in northeastern Brazil.
interestingFacts: ["Distinguished by a sharp, deep sagittal cranial crest that curved downward along the premaxilla at a unique 45-degree angle.","Features unusually deep premaxillary margins and short, toothless, downturned jaws specialized for harvesting hard prehistoric fruits.","Named in honor of both the indigenous Kariri ethnic nation and the comic book heroine Diana Prince (Wonder Woman).","Belongs to the Tapejarinae, an endemic clade of ornate-crested pterosaurs that diversified rapidly across Gondwana."]
sizeNotes: Tapejarid pterosaur with a well-preserved skull and jaws exhibiting an estimated wingspan of approximately 2.5 meters. Note: Wingspan 3.0 m noted. Quadrupedal body length 1.0 m, standing height 0.9 m, mass 5 kg (Cerqueira et al. 2021).

name: Jormungandr
dietDetails: Apex marine predator preying on cephalopods, hesperornithiform diving birds, sea turtles, and bony fish.
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Pembina Gorge, North Dakota","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Pierre Shale Formation"}
discoveryHistory: Found in 2015 along the Pembina River in Cavalier County, North Dakota, and described in 2023 by Amelia Zietlow, Clint Boyd, and Mark Norell.
interestingFacts: ["Represents a crucial 'missing link' mosasaur documenting how plioplatecarpines transitioned into apex giants like Mosasaurus.","Retained primitive characteristics including 11 ribs above the pelvis while evolving advanced, crushing jaw morphology.","Inhabited the frigid, nutrient-rich waters of the Western Interior Seaway which split North America in half.","Its fossil skull preserves distinct rugose brow ridges above the eye sockets that may have supported protective structures."]
sizeNotes: Transitional mosasaur exhibiting an intermediate mosaic of primitive Clidastes-like and advanced Mosasaurus-like cranial traits.
